instructor: YUAN, George Jie; TANG TANG, Raymundo Saijong
content_text:
Course Outline:
Chapter 1: Signals and Systems
Chapter 2: Digital Systems
Chapter 3: Digitization
Chapter 4: Coding of Digital Information
Chapter 5: Communications
Chapter 6: The Internet

It's a great introductory CC course to learn related topics if you have no prior knowledge. Nevertheless, due to this course's popularity, you probably can only enrol this course in your senior year. When you finally enrolled, your classmate will likely be a year 4 Engineering student who has already learnt 75% of the course and just wants to fulfil the SSC-S&T CC requirement.
teaching_text:
Another semester with online lectures via Zoom 🙂.

I didn't attend many lectures. The professor mostly read from the slides.

Tang Tang is a great tutor who can explain concepts clearly. I recommend you to attend the tutorial if you decide to take this course.
grading_text:
Grading Scheme:
Homework: 10% (2% each)
Midterm (Online): 45%
Final Exam (Online): 45%

There is an optional group project with 2 people in a group create a ppt introducing a technology. If your group get 8/10 or above, your final grade will be one sub-grade up.
workload_text:
The workload is small, only 5 homework which can be finished within 2 hours. Most homework problems are taught in tutorials so make sure to check the tutorial notes.

I'm not sure about the workload of the project.
There is no attendance.

However, you need to spend extra time to revise the material before the exam if it is the first time you encounter these topics.

content_text:
People with DSE Physics background will only have slight advantage, but not big enough to completely carry them.

Starting with some chill explanations on circuit components, then here comes KCL and KVL, where having some math intuition will help for calculating currents in complex circuits.

Diode and transistors are also new. Good news is you don't need to know why it works, just know how it works. This goes the same for H-bridge and motor design.

Final part is logic control, where instead of using logic gates, you use Arduino to control your car.

After learning everything, you now have to build a small robot car for the project, which it needs to follow a map. Honestly quite fun.
teaching_text:
Profess Lin is meh. He has a strange accent which doesn't help the fact the lectures were somewhat boring. It's hard to focus on a 9:30 am lecture.

Ms Tang is ok. Strong mainland accent, but she reviews the content quite well in tutorials so the pros and cons balance well.

But do you know why this is getting a B instead of C? It's because the lab assistant were FUCKING AWESOME. Very helpful, very friendly, couldn't have made it out without him.
grading_text:
Lab 30%
Pop-quiz 10%
Lab Exam 15%
Written Exam 20%
Project (Robot car) 20%
Project Report 5%

Student's score: 95.1% → A+

Grading can vary significantly by semester (this semester was relatively lenient).
workload_text: The main workload is the robot car project (two stages on the map). Many students struggled at stage 1 U-turn. Other components are relatively light.

course_title: Information Technology Revolution: Past, Present and Future
content_text: Broad overview of IT history and concepts: transistor, Claude Shannon & information theory, computing generations, internet, security, algorithms, emerging trends, entrepreneurship, programming basics & Generative AI. Content feels a bit scattered/messy.
teaching_text: Prof. Guan is nice and willing to answer questions. Lectures are mostly reading from slides and can be a bit boring.
grading_text: In-lecture quiz 4%, Post-lecture quiz 14%, Coding quiz 10%, Coding Project 10%, Presentation (PPT 5% + delivery 10% + summary 6% + peer review 5%), Final exam 36%. Strict grade cutoffs (A+ starts at 97).
workload_text: Moderate workload. Weekly quizzes, one relatively easy coding project, presentation preparation, open-book final exam.

course_title: A System View of Communications: from Signals to Packets
content_text:
Over a total of 24 lectures covering signals, systems and networking.

Lecture topics include: Basic signal transmission, LTI systems, Protocols, BER & Eye Diagrams, Channel modelling, Equalization, Gaussian noise, Channel coding, Fourier series, Spectrograms, FDM, Networking layers (Link, Network, Transport, Application).

Labs (7 labs + post-lab quiz): MATLAB basics, Modelling Channels, Communication protocol, Eye Diagram & Equalization, SNR & BER, Time-frequency analysis, Frequency division multiplexing.

Concepts are not too difficult but the pace is quite fast. Make your own notes because lecture slides are not detailed enough.
teaching_text: Prof MURCH is friendly and welcomes questions during lecture or office hours. IA is also nice.
grading_text:
Lab Checkpoints 10%
Lab Quizzes 15%
3 Homeworks 10%
Midterm 25%
Final Exam 40%

Student example: C grade (detailed HW, quiz and exam scores provided in review). No calculators allowed in exams.
workload_text: Quite light workload for a 4-credit course. Main effort is understanding concepts and completing labs. No project this semester. Strongly recommend making your own notes.

content_text: 22 topics covered including Complex Numbers, Impulse Response, Convolution, Fourier Series (CT/DT), Fourier Transform (CT/DT), Sampling, Laplace Transform, etc. Content is quite challenging, especially CT/DT Fourier Transforms. Requires strong understanding of mathematical concepts. Good foundation for signal processing.
teaching_text: Prof. Yobas teaches clearly but voice is not very loud. IA CHANG Mang Yee (MY) is excellent in tutorials - highly recommended to attend. She revises key concepts and helps with questions.
grading_text: Homework 18%, Labs 12%, Midterm 25%, Final 45%. Student scored A (84.845/100) with strong HW and Lab performance.
workload_text: 6 Homeworks + 4 Lab assignments. Moderate workload compared to other courses. Recommend starting homework early and attending prelabs. Exams are similar to homework questions.

course_title: Introduction to Computer Organization and Design
content_text:
L0 Course introduction
L1 Introduction
L2 Computer Arithmetic
L3 Instruction Program (MIPS)
L4 Arithmetics II (IEEE754)
L5 Computer performance
L6 Single Cycle Processor
L7 Pipeline Processor
L8 Memory

Content is much lighter than COMP2611 (no heavy programming). Concepts are straightforward but require attention to detail.
teaching_text: Prof. XIE explains content very clearly with good interaction and review at the start of each lecture. Strict on discipline and sometimes runs overtime. IA Vivian is excellent, responsive, and gives clear tutorials.
grading_text:
10% HW (2 assignments)
20% Lab (4 labs)
25% Midterm
45% Final

Exams are manageable if you are careful; many questions are similar to COMP2611 homework.
workload_text: Very light workload for a 4-credit course (feels like 2 credits). Main effort is on 2 HWs + 4 labs. No project this semester.

instructor: CHAU, Kevin; CHOI, Ricky Yiu Kee
content_text: Week 1-12 covers: Fundamental Concepts, KCL/KVL, DC Analysis, Thevenin/Norton theorems, AC Circuits, Op Amp, Frequency Response (Bode plot), Transient Analysis, Diode Circuits.\n\nConsidered one of the easier ELEC 2000-level courses if you have PHYS1114 background.
teaching_text: Prof. Chau explains fundamentals very well. TA Ricky is very good and helpful in tutorials.
grading_text: HW*5 10%, Lab*5 20%, Midterm 25%, Final 45%. Student scored 83.55% → A. Grading is fair with guaranteed A-range percentage.
workload_text: Moderate workload. 5 HWs and 5 Labs. HWs can be time-consuming (especially complex numbers). Labs require advance preparation and bringing kit home.

instructor: SRIVASTAVA, Abhishek Kumar; CHOI, Ricky Yiu Kee
content_text: Simplified version of ELEC2400 for non-ECE students. Covers fundamentals, DC analysis (KCL/KVL, superposition, Thevenin/Norton), Op Amps, transient analysis with capacitors, binary arithmetic, Boolean algebra, combinational and sequential logic (latches, flip-flops).
teaching_text: Prof. Srivastava teaches decently with passion. TA Dr. Ricky Choi is excellent, humorous, and very helpful.
grading_text: HW 10%, Labs 15%, Midterm 20%, Final 55%. Exams are straightforward if you understand concepts.
workload_text: Very light workload. 7 homeworks (recycled questions), 3 simple labs. Easy if you follow the lectures.

course_title: Probability and Random Processes in Engineering
content_text: Boring content that focuses on memorising and applying formulas without deep understanding of the underlying principles. MATH probability courses are better for real understanding (but much harder).
teaching_text: Prof. Wong's lectures are quite boring and confusing. Better to study lecture notes yourself and only watch recordings when needed. He is a nice person by personality.
grading_text:
Homework Assignments 8%
Laboratory Exercises 12%
Mid-term 30%
Final 50%

Student example: Midterm 91 (+1.7 SD), Final 74.5 (+1 SD) → overall ~84.5% → A
workload_text: Medium workload for a 4-credit course. 4 assignments + 5 lab exercises. Assignments are useful for exams; labs teach Matplotlib (not tested).

content_text:
Lecture topics: Discrete-Time Signals & Systems, DTFT, DFT, FFT, z-Transform, FIR Filter Design, Source Coding, Channel Coding, Baseband Communications, Digital Modulation, Signal Space, Channel Models, Multiplexing.

Labs: CT/DT signals, DFT, Convolution & Filter, Information theory, BER simulation.

Content is solid but requires good understanding of the concepts.
teaching_text: Prof. Zhang explains concepts patiently and in detail. He writes many notes on PPT and uploads annotated versions after every lecture — extremely helpful for revision.
grading_text: HW 15% (2 assignments), Lab 10% (4 exercises), Midterm 30%, Final 45%. Student scored A+ (high marks in HW/Lab/Midterm). Grading is kind.
workload_text: Kind of heavy workload. Few but time-consuming HWs and labs. Need to fully understand the material for exams. Labs require attendance to get marks.

content_text: The course material is based on CMU lecture notes, though I’m not sure the CMU lecture videos would help much. He was a TA there a few years back, so the style here feels a bit different.\n\nYou’ll go through all the layers of networking, from the physical layer up to the application layer. The big focus is on TCP, and you’ll actually have to implement it from scratch, which is where most of the heavy lifting happens.
teaching_text:
I’d say he’s basically the Desmond of ECE. He’s got that same passion for teaching that makes you feel like he actually cares, which is more than I can say for quite a few other profs here (yes especially you kty).

I don’t know if he lives inside his outlook inbox or what, but whenever you email him, you’ll almost always get a reply within five minutes on a normal school day. Even on weekends, he’ll usually get back to you within an hour.

He’s super willing to chat and actually gives useful insights, unlike some professors who just forward your email to the TAs.

Project 1 was kind of a pain, but he didn’t leave us hanging. Right before the CP1 deadline, a bunch of us camped out in his office...
workload_text:
Project 0 was basically free marks. All you had to do was leave your computer on for 24 hours...

Most of the coursework can be wrapped up in under two hours, except for Project 1. That one takes way longer...

Project 1 is no joke, you have to implement the entire TCP stack... For Fall 2024, though, he promised to drop the handshake requirement and simplify a few sections.

content_text: Week 1-13 topics: Introduction, Transforms (Fourier, Sampling), Morphological Processing, Image Enhancement (Spatial & Frequency), Restoration (filters), Color Processing, Compression, Predictive Coding, Segmentation, Object Recognition, Face Detection (Eigenface, LDA). Math-heavy but very fruitful.
teaching_text: Prof. Wang explains clearly and reminds students of important notes. TAs are helpful but sometimes not fully familiar with the content.
grading_text: HW 20% (3 assignments), Midterm 30%, Final Project 50% (20% Presentation + 30% Report). Student scored A+ (strong HW + Midterm).
workload_text: Moderate-to-heavy workload. 3 HWs (some complex MATLAB parts) + group final project (3-5 people, requires code submission). Need to plan time well.

content_text: Very math-oriented course covering state-space concepts, modeling, linearization, Laplace transform, transfer functions, block diagrams, stability (Routh criterion, pole placement), root locus, feedback control, PID, etc. Exams are generally easier than homework problems.
teaching_text: Prof. Shen explains concepts clearly and is responsive to questions after lectures and via email. First time teaching the course but did well.
grading_text: HW 20% (4 assignments), Midterm 30% (open book), Final 50% (open book), Optional Labs 5% (bonus). Average UST grading. Student scored A (Midterm 80/100, Final 90/100).
workload_text: Light workload for a 4-credit course. Main effort is on 4 homeworks (can be tedious with calculations). Exams are open book; bring laptop + online calculators.

content_text: Lectures focus mostly on concepts with limited practical guidance. Students must figure out most implementation themselves in labs. The final group project is extremely demanding, stressful, and the main pain point of the course.
teaching_text: Prof. Woo is nice but lectures are boring. Main TA explains labs and project reasonably well but has very high standards for creativity and complexity.
grading_text: IPRS 8%, Assignments 10%, Labs 18%, Project 64% (proposal, interim demo, final demo & presentation, report). Project grading is very harsh.
workload_text: Extremely heavy workload dominated by the final project. Requires significant time, creativity, hardware knowledge, debugging, and often extra money for components. Many students (especially beginners) find it overwhelming.

instructor: YOBAS, Levent; TANG TANG, Raymundo Saijong
content_text: Revamped version of ELEC2200. Uses Vivado Design Suite + Basys 3 Artix-7 FPGA Board.\n\nCovers: Introductory concepts, Boolean algebra, Combinational logic (adders, MUX/DEMUX, etc.), Sequential logic (latches, flip-flops), Finite State Machines (Mealy/Moore, counters, sequence detectors).
teaching_text: Prof. Yobas explains thoroughly in small class. TA does great job reviewing VHDL syntax and lab assignments.
grading_text: Attendance + extra points, short homeworks, 7 lab assignments, Midterm exam, Final exam, Miniproject.
workload_text: Not heavy workload. Must attend all lab sessions or you fail. Skeleton VHDL codes provided. Do labs in advance because Vivado synthesis/implementation takes time.

course_title: Introduction to Integrated Circuits and Systems
content_text: Covers IC industry overview, Diodes, BJT & MOSFET transistors, small signal analysis, single/multi-stage amplifiers, differential amplifiers. Uses Hspice for simulation. Requires strong KCL/KVL and ELEC2400 background.
teaching_text: Prof. Luong explains clearly with good pace and repeats key points. Reminds students of admin matters regularly.
grading_text: 5 HW 10% (4 counted), Class participation 5%, 3 Labs 20%, Midterm 25%, Final Project 40%. Student scored A+ with strong performance.
workload_text: Heavy workload. HWs involve hand calculations + Hspice simulation. Final group project requires designing a differential amplifier from scratch. Labs require prelab and report.

content_text: Basics of semiconductor, diodes, MOSFET, small signal analysis, amplifiers etc. Blended learning with pre-lecture videos. Content is conceptual and somewhat abstract.
teaching_text: Blended learning with pre-lecture videos (good animations but quite condensed). Prof. Shao explains well during revision and solution discussions.
grading_text: 5 HW 10%, Labs, Pre-lecture quizzes, Biweekly quizzes, iPRs, Final exam. +10% bonus for completing daily components. Student scored A- (75 overall).
workload_text: Workload depends on goal. Light if just passing, but quite heavy if aiming for good grade (pre-lecture videos, tricky quizzes, HW, labs).

course_title: Electromagnetics: From Wireless to Photonic Applications
content_text: Foundational EE course covering vector algebra/calculus, electrostatics, magnetostatics, Maxwell’s equations, EM wave propagation, transmission lines etc. Very important for EE masters/PhD, IC design, microelectronics or photonics. Calculus-heavy (choosing best integrals and coordinates).
teaching_text: Prof. Poon explains in great detail and is very patient. Repeats parts if students don’t understand and gives long, detailed email replies.
grading_text: 80% Homework (8 assignments), 20% Quizzes (4 quizzes), 15% optional project (bonus). Student scored 91% → A.
workload_text: Manageable workload. No midterm or final exam. Revise weekly and do the assignments (they force you to review the material).

content_text: Probability & statistics, statistical detection/estimation, random processes, neural signals, encoding/decoding, population coding, neural networks, supervised & reinforcement learning, neural prosthesis & rehabilitation.
teaching_text: Prof. Wang explains concepts very clearly and ties together math, neuroscience and machine learning effectively.
grading_text: 4 Homework assignments 20%, Midterm 30%, Final Project 50%. HWs are manageable (can finish in one evening each). Midterm very similar to HW1/HW2.
workload_text: Manageable workload. HWs are straightforward. Final project is reasonable with good planning.

instructor: WONG, Kai Sun Albert; CHOW, Cupid
content_text: Basic business concepts for engineers: accounting, management, supply chain, marketing, financial statements, options/interest/futures. Very easy (like simplified DSE Econ).
teaching_text: Prof. Wong and Cupid teach clearly. Lectures are straightforward (mostly reading slides with some stories).
grading_text: 20% In-class exercises, 30% 4 Assignments, 50% Final exam (open-book with restrictions). Grading is lenient.
workload_text: Light workload. 4 easy assignments + one final exam. No heavy project or labs.

content_text: Builds on ELEC3100. Covers M-ary modulation, signal space, wireless channels, small-scale fading, diversity techniques, ISI mitigation, resource partitioning (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA), 5G and beyond.
teaching_text: Prof. Lau teaches excellently with clear explanations. TAs (Miss Zhuang and Mr Zhai) are extremely poor — irresponsible, bad teaching, terrible course management (delayed grading, marking errors, sudden deadline changes).
grading_text: 3 Assignments 15%, Project 10%, Midterm 25%, Final 50%. Grading can feel inconsistent/unfair due to TA issues.
workload_text: Manageable workload. 3 HW + group project (can use AI). Midterm and final are the main challenges.

content_text: Introduction to robot anatomy, kinematics (forward & inverse), reactive behaviors, motion planning, robot components. Labs on robot arm (RoArm-M1) and quadruped robot (Mangdang Mini Pupper). Open-book exams with questions very similar to practice.
teaching_text: Prof. Zhang teaches clearly with good English accent.
grading_text: Midterm 30%, Homework 25% (4 sets, best 3 count), Lab 15%, Final 30%. Homework and labs are easy to get full marks.
workload_text: Light workload. One lecture per week, easy group lab reports, manageable assignments.

content_text: Basically a copy of Stanford CS231N. Covers convolutional networks, object detection, segmentation, GANs, diffusion models etc. Faster pace than COMP4211, includes more advanced architectures. Some weeks had guest lectures / PhD talks.
teaching_text: Prof. Chen is knowledgeable but lectures are dry (9am slot + mostly reading slides). Many students sleep or skip. Better to supplement with Stanford CS231N YouTube videos (new and old versions).
grading_text: 3 Programming Assignments (PAs), Midterm exam, Final Project (3 reports + presentation). Most people get full marks on PAs. Midterm is a big differentiator (mean ~55).
workload_text: Moderate to heavy workload. 3 PAs (skeleton code provided, 1-2 days each if just completing, longer if learning deeply) + project with LaTeX reports.

course_title: FPGA-based Design: From Theory to Practice
content_text: 4 Labs + 3 HWs + Project (Midterm cancelled this semester). Labs require filling in Verilog code; last two labs quite difficult. Project needs proposal + report.
teaching_text: Lectures a bit boring (professor spends time on single slides) but she kindly answers questions. Learn most during lab sessions if you have basic FPGA knowledge.
grading_text: Typical ELEC grading, mean around B.
workload_text: Moderate workload. Time-consuming labs (especially if new to Verilog), homeworks, and project report.

course_title: Analogue Integrated Circuits Design and Analysis
content_text: Covers chapters 1-6, 8-10 of Razavi’s book: frequency response, feedback, operational amplifiers, compensation etc.
teaching_text: Prof. Zhang teaches excellently with clear derivations on whiteboard. Lectures are important to attend.
grading_text: 20% Homework (3 assignments), 30% Midterm, 50% Project. Good grading; A+ for top 3 projects.
workload_text: Light workload for a 4-credit course. Assignments take about 1 day each. Project uses Cadence Virtuoso.

content_text: Power Computation, Rectifier, Switch Mode Power Converters (DC-DC), basic Control and Feedback, Magnetism. Content is relatively light/not very deep.
teaching_text: Prof. Man explains clearly and is willing to help students.
grading_text: 3 Assignments 12%, Project 1 22%, Project 2 26%, Final Exam 40%. Most people score high on assignments and projects. Final exam mean ~47/100.
workload_text: Easy assignments and projects. Final exam is closed book. No laboratory sessions.

content_text: Covers geometrical optics, lenses, aberrations, physical optics, wave theory, diffraction, interference, polarization, optical instruments (cameras, microscopes, telescopes). Interesting introductory optics course.
teaching_text: Prof. Qu explains clearly. No lecture recordings — attendance is encouraged.
grading_text: 15% HW, 15% Lab reports, 20% Midterm, 50% Final. Student scored A+ (HW 93.6%, Lab 96.83%, Midterm 82.5%, Final 97%).
workload_text: Very light workload. Attend lectures, complete HW and lab reports. Exams are straightforward with cheetsheet allowed for some proofs.

content_text: Optoelectronics and fiber optics for communications: optical fibers, sources, detectors, passive components for WDM. Hands-on labs building wavelength-division-multiplexed optical links.
teaching_text: Prof. Poon is extremely nice, patient, and one of the best teachers in ECE.
grading_text: 6 HW 30%, 6 Labs 24%, Project (term paper 10% + presentation 6%) 16%, Final exam 30%.
workload_text: Heavy workload ('NO PAIN, NO GAIN'). Frequent HW, long labs (full 3 hours), term paper + final exam.

content_text: Heavy on biology + electronics: biopotentials (ECG/EMG/EEG), blood pressure/flow, respiratory monitors (capnography, oximetry), clinical chemistry, integrated biosensors. Includes circuit design for biosignal measurement.
teaching_text: Prof. Qu's teaching is boring and not engaging if you are not interested in biology + electronics.
grading_text: Homework, labs (strict grading on reports), Midterm, Final. Student scored B.
workload_text: Quite heavy workload at the beginning (weekly HW + labs + prelabs). Later HW becomes meaningless. Final exam requires good understanding of circuits.

content_text: Basic principles of medical imaging modalities: X-ray projection, CT, SPECT/PET, ultrasound, MRI + some application examples. Heavy on math (geometry, linear algebra, calculus, signals & systems, Fourier Transform).
teaching_text: Blended learning style: self-study material beforehand + weekly discussion class. Professor and TAs are nice but many students get lost when studying alone.
grading_text: 10% Homework, 10% Online quiz, 10% Attendance & discussion participation, 30% Mid-term, 40% Final. Bonus points for answering discussion questions.
workload_text: Very light workload. Easy weekly quiz, several assignments (many from reference book), optional discussion questions for bonus.

course_title: Artificial Intelligence for Medical Image Analysis
content_text: Deep learning for medical image analysis: classification, detection, segmentation, 3D/multi-modality images, retinal, ultrasound, pathology etc. Covers DNN fundamentals and advanced topics (self-supervised learning, generative modeling, vision foundation models). Similar to Stanford CS231N but focused on medical applications.
teaching_text: Very good teaching.
grading_text: 3 Assignments + Final Project. Student scored A- (high marks on assignments and 92.5/100 on project).
workload_text: Hard assignments but overall manageable workload.

content_text: Introductory programming using Python 3 + PyGame. Covers basics, control flow, functions, arrays, recursion, data structures (list, tuple, dict), Turtle graphics, object-oriented programming, file I/O.
teaching_text: Prof. Gibson Lam teaches clearly with good examples. Lectures are useful and the course website is well-organized.
grading_text: Midterm 20%, Final 40%, Assignments 40% (Music System + Game Project). Grading is fair but assignments require effort.
workload_text: Manageable workload for an introductory course. Labs are not graded, but assignments (especially the game project) take time. No heavy project or presentation.

content_text: Comprehensive C++ course: basics, control flow, functions, arrays, recursion, pointers, dynamic memory, linked lists, binary trees, classes, stack/queue. Very strong foundation if you have no prior C++ experience.
teaching_text: Both instructors are excellent. Gary builds solid understanding; Chatzopoulos gives lots of practice. Lectures are highly recommended.
grading_text: Labs 10%, Programming Assignments 37%, Quiz 8%, Final Exam 45%. Exams are tough but fair if you understand the material.
workload_text: Heavy workload if new to C++. Labs and 3 Programming Assignments (PA1–PA3) take significant time, especially recursion, pointers, linked lists, and trees.
